name: Pyrilutamide
lead: Pyrilutamide, developmental code KX-826, is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor antagonist designed for topical use in androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss) and acne. It is being developed by Suzhou Kintor Pharmaceuticals [1][2]. Wikipedia describes it as a high-affinity, selective silent antagonist of the androgen receptor [1].

As of early 2025 Wikipedia lists it in phase 3 trials for hair loss and phase 2 for acne, and it has not been approved as a drug by a major regulator [1]. According to Grokipedia, a phase 3 trial in Chinese men met its primary endpoint versus baseline but not versus placebo, and cosmetic formulations were launched in China in July 2024 [2].
Discussion in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums groups it with RU58841 as an experimental topical anti-androgen, and some users describe obtaining it outside regulated channels [3][4].

paras: The compound is investigated for androgenetic alopecia in men and women and for acne vulgaris. A diabetic foot ulcer programme was discontinued [1]. Topical antiandrogens are positioned in review literature as candidates to avoid the systemic effects of oral antiandrogens and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors [5][6].

Two phase 1 studies registered on ClinicalTrials.gov tested single and multiple ascending topical doses of KX-826 in 40 healthy men each with androgenetic alopecia, with safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics as the aims [7][8]. Grokipedia reports that adverse events were mostly mild application-site reactions, with minimal systemic exposure [2].

Per Grokipedia, a Chinese phase 2 study in women reported a target-area hair count increase of 11.39 hairs per cm2 versus placebo at 24 weeks for 0.5% once daily, and a US phase 2 study in men reported a 15.34 hairs per cm2 increase from baseline at 24 weeks for 0.5% twice daily, with positive trends versus placebo [2]. The same source reports that the registrational Chinese phase 3 trial in men met its endpoint versus baseline but did not reach statistical significance versus placebo, and that later work tested a 1.0% concentration and a combination with minoxidil [2]. These results are drawn from company announcements summarised by a non-peer-reviewed encyclopedia, and peer-reviewed full reports are limited.

Pyrilutamide competes with dihydrotestosterone for the androgen receptor [1][2]. A 2026 medicinal chemistry paper used pyrilutamide as a benchmark for new topical 'soft drug' antagonists designed to be rapidly inactivated if absorbed, reporting comparable efficacy in a mouse hair-growth model [9]. Grokipedia reports rapid skin distribution and low plasma exposure in animal and early human work [2].

Trial adverse events are reported as mild and mostly local, such as redness, itching or dryness [2]. Long-term human data are limited. A forum user on T Nation described experiencing unusual side effects after roughly three weeks of use and asked for guidance on recovery, an individual report that has not been verified [4].

The compound is not approved as a drug, and cosmetic products in China were described by Grokipedia as launched in 2024 [2]. Forum posters mention it alongside RU58841 as non-FDA-approved topical anti-androgens that must be continued to maintain results [3].

timeline.event: Cosmetic formulations launched in China, per Grokipedia [2].
Wikipedia lists phase 3 trials for hair loss [1].

lore.intro: Community material on pyrilutamide is sparse and appears mainly as brief mentions on T Nation alongside RU58841 [3][4].

claims.claim: Pyrilutamide is a topical anti-androgen that works like RU58841 for hair
claims.believers: A T Nation poster lists it with RU-58841 as topical anti-androgens that work, noting they are not FDA approved and must be maintained [3].
claims.experts: Company-reported phase 2 data show hair count gains, while the phase 3 trial in Chinese men reportedly did not separate from placebo; no published comparison with RU58841 exists [2].

claims.claim: A topical anti-androgen cannot cause systemic side effects
claims.believers: Proponents point to its design for rapid local metabolism as limiting systemic action [2].
claims.experts: Early trials reported minimal plasma levels and mild adverse events, but one forum user reported unusual symptoms after short use, and long-term data are limited [2][4].
